title: Block close: reforms
hook: Protestants and Catholics both reformed, both failed, both produced saints

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sunday schools, reading lessons on the one free day for working children. Your line was every child can learn. What did you teach, and who learned it? Day nine hundred fifteen.

Lay out the faces from this block on a table, like old photographs. A monk with a list of theses for debate. A Dutchman turning back across the ice to pull his pursuer out. A soldier with a shattered leg reading saints' lives in bed. A nun on a dusty road founding small, poor convents. A man at the stake, praying for a king's eyes to be opened. A tinker writing in a jail cell. A preacher in a field. Some of them would not have shared a table with each other. Their churches put each other's people to death. And here they are, on one table, in one story. Today: the block close.

This block began with a church that needed reform, and with the line: always reforming. It ends with three honest sentences. Both reformed. Luther, Calvin, Menno Simons and Cranmer pressed for a church grounded in scripture, in the people's own language. Trent, Ignatius, Teresa and Francis de Sales renewed the Catholic Church from the inside: better trained priests, deeper prayer, gentler pastors. Both failed. Protestants executed Catholics and drowned Anabaptists. Catholics burned Protestants. Massacres in Paris, a war that tore Europe apart, kings using faith for power. Christians on each side did things this block could not soften. Both produced saints. Dirk Willems on the ice. Thomas More keeping his conscience. Vincent de Paul and Louise de Marillac feeding the poor. Wesley on horseback, starting the Methodist movement. Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, writing about a burden that rolls away. And outside Europe, people like Las Casas, Kateri and Richard Allen carrying the same faith into very different lives. The book of Lamentations says: "Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD." The verse says our ways, not theirs. Some Reformed Christians use a phrase for this: a church reformed, and always being reformed. Catholics speak of the church always in need of purifying. And in John's Gospel, Jesus prays for his followers "That they all may be one". Some churches today tell this story together more than they used to, Protestants and Catholics admitting their own side's wounds. That is part of the reform too.

Here's the practice: pray for someone from the other side, or simply wish them well. Let your breath slow. Bring to mind one person on the other side of a divide from you. Another church, another faith, another politics, another side of a family quarrel. Hold the person, not their opinions. Then think of one thing on your own side that needs reform. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, and for yourself. If you don't, just wish them good. The bell holds the time.
Lamentations. The book whose line, let us search and try our ways, this block borrows to look honestly at its own reforms, failures, and saints.

Your line: reformed and reforming. Today, say one kind and true thing about a church or group you don't belong to. Tomorrow a new block begins: the modern church across the world. Day nine hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Protestant and Catholic churches hold joint services and dialogues, and some have issued shared statements on the Reformation that admit wrongs on their own side.

Hook: 'a man in the flames, praying for a king's eyes to be opened' is Tyndale (866), who tradition says was strangled before burning; confirm the image is acceptable. 'Protestants executed Catholics and drowned Anabaptists' (Felix Manz, 860): confirm.
'Ecclesia reformata, semper reformanda' attributed only to 'some Reformed Christians'; Vatican II's 'semper purificanda' (Lumen Gentium 8) framed as 'Catholics speak of'. Confirm.
howItsDone: joint statements (e.g. the Lutheran–Catholic 'From Conflict to Communion') are general; confirm.

Editor pass: 'some of them burned each other' was untrue of the people listed, so it now says their churches put each other's people to death; 'a man in the flames' became 'a man at the stake' (Tyndale was strangled before burning); 'churches today' became 'some churches today'; the practice drops the repeated 'picture their face' image.
Second editor pass: practice opener varied ('Settle, and breathe' was repeated across days 908–916).

Audit pass: untangled 'and the line always reforming'; replaced the narrator's verdict 'that is what reform means at its best' with a plain reading of the verse. Keeper: Thomas More is listed among the saints; he also pursued Protestants as chancellor. Consider whether the list needs that note for fairness.
